digests.narrative: The theme got a number this week, and it came from the sell side rather than from the companies. Goldman Sachs raised its global optical module forecast to $67.7bn for 2026 (+33%), $131.4bn for 2027 (+81%) and $148.5bn for 2028 (+115%), lifted its 1.6T-and-above 2027 forecast by 61%, and modelled 80% silicon photonics penetration. The mechanism matters more than the total: it raised optical modules per GPU on Rubin Ultra, 1.6T from zero to two and 3.2T from three to five, so more optical content ships per chip regardless of how many chips ship. Per that report a 1.6T silicon photonics module carries four 70mW CW lasers at roughly $3.75-5 each, which is precisely the part the shortage is in. Citi went further and called lasers and optical fibre the next HBM, with tight supply supporting a scarcity premium. Then the confirmation arrived from the ground rather than from a model. A crowdsourced channel check at CIOE Shenzhen reported Sivers actively engaged with Chinese pluggable makers and, more importantly, raising laser prices, with 70mW parts the tightest because they sit in 800G pluggables. Chinese pluggable maker CIG's own filings describe substantially longer delivery times and deposits required to secure capacity; Innolight is signing multi-supplier laser LTAs. Sivers separately announced Glasgow InP expansion targeting over 100m CW DFB lasers a year from Q4 2027 — which the analyst models at $625m-$1.25bn of capacity revenue at historical ASPs, explicitly illustrative rather than guidance. The structural point he makes about Lumentum is the one to hold: Cloud Light expanded its served datacentre opportunity more than fivefold, so a laser company does not have to stay a laser company. Against all that, the desk's own reservations from 1 Sep are unchanged — Lumentum's $7.76bn convertible extinguishment, AAOI's $1.03bn of ATM issuance, and Sivers' shrinking reported sales. Better TAM does not fix a share count or a cash burn.
keyPoints: Goldman raised optical module TAM to $131.4bn for 2027 (+81%) and $148.5bn for 2028 (+115%)
Optical content per GPU raised on Rubin Ultra: 1.6T modules 0 to 2, 3.2T 3 to 5
A 1.6T silicon photonics module carries four 70mW CW lasers — the exact part in shortage
Citi TMT: lasers and optical fibre are the next HBM, with a scarcity premium on tight supply
CIOE Shenzhen channel check: Sivers has raised laser prices; 70mW is the tightest part
CIG's filings describe longer lead times and deposits to secure laser capacity

digests.narrative: Memory spent the week producing the tightest supply data this desk has recorded, and the two stocks that own it spent it 38% below their peaks. SED reports Samsung and SK hynix stockpiles have fallen below ten days of supply. KB Securities expects the tightest supply conditions in history next year and projects memory's share of AI infrastructure cost rising from 40% this year to 57% next; TrendForce puts that figure at 68%. Japanese distributors quoted in Nikkei put the demand deficit at 40-60%, meaning demand running 67-150% above supply, with general prices up 50% by year end. The legacy tier is where this is already showing up in reported revenue rather than forecast: August revenues came in at ESMT +605% year on year, Etron +525%, Winbond +289% and Macronix +218.5%, with Etron's chairman seeing momentum extending through 2028 and possibly 2030, and Winbond's president expecting 2027 tighter than 2026. The analyst's framing is the useful one — this is the only industry where every investor cheers for shortages — and his arithmetic on why legacy pricing sticks is the sharpest thing in the file: a DDR2 chip at roughly $0.96 tripling in price adds about $2 to the bill of materials of a $33 security camera, which no buyer refuses, while being transformative to the supplier. The desk's position is unchanged and is about price, not demand. SanDisk's 71.5% gross margin is a cycle peak against 16.1% two years ago, its top ten customers are 44% of revenue with none above 10%, and no contracted volume defends that margin. Both stocks falling 38% while the shortage data got better is either the market pricing a peak or the same duration unwind visible across the book.
keyPoints: Samsung and SK hynix stockpiles reported below ten days of supply
KB Securities: tightest memory supply in history next year; memory rises to 57% of AI infra cost
Nikkei-quoted distributors put the demand deficit at 40-60%, prices up 50% by year end
Legacy August revenue: ESMT +605%, Etron +525%, Winbond +289%, Macronix +218.5% year on year
Winbond expects 2027 tighter than 2026; Etron sees momentum to 2028-2030
MU and SK hynix fell 38% from peaks while every supply datapoint improved

digests.narrative: The week's framing was geopolitical rather than operational, and it favours the incumbents. The analyst laid out where the genuine monopolies actually sit, and almost none are American: ASML in EUV with Zeiss and Trumpf beneath it, Soitec in photonics-SOI, and a Japanese cluster holding 90-100% share across EUV photoresist, coat and develop, actinic mask inspection, mask blanks and specialty glass. The United States holds EDA, some equipment and the downstream giants; Taiwan and Korea hold the manufacturing. Read against China halting some rare earth shipments, the point is that chokepoints are distributed across allies rather than concentrated in one country, and that every participant has something to withhold. TSMC remains the centre of it and the analyst maintains his bullish stance despite Intel and Samsung competition, on the argument that everyone including Marvell and all of big tech is reliant on it and that it has demonstrated the ability to raise prices, which flows to margin. TSMC's own guidance that silicon photonics goes mainstream in 2027 with more than half the optical transceiver market is the specific claim to hold it for. GlobalFoundries' SCALE platform is the photonic foundry layer of the same shift, still with no attached revenue and an H2 2027 to 2028 horizon. Intel adds a small near-term item, reportedly raising PC CPU prices 10% in October, which is pricing power in a business nobody credits with any.
keyPoints: The real monopolies are mostly non-US: ASML in EUV, Soitec in photonics-SOI, a Japanese cluster at 90-100% share
China halting some rare earth shipments underlines that every bloc holds something to withhold
TSMC guides silicon photonics mainstream in 2027 at over half the optical transceiver market
TSMC has demonstrated price increases, which flow straight to margin
GF SCALE remains the photonic foundry layer with no revenue attached yet
Intel reportedly raising PC CPU prices 10% in October

digests.narrative: Nebius got the company-specific catalyst the desk said was missing. Palantir named it a preferred sovereign AI infrastructure partner, which routes Palantir's existing US government and enterprise relationships toward Nebius capacity rather than toward the hyperscalers. On 1 Sep the desk held at wait explicitly because the week's neocloud news had been good for the category and specific to a competitor — Anthropic's $35bn compute deal with NVIDIA-backed Lambda. This is the opposite case, and it is the kind of contract the desk said would justify revisiting. Two things temper it. The partnership is a preferred-partner designation rather than a disclosed contract value, so there is no revenue number to underwrite, and the analyst's own framing of the category still applies: NVIDIA helps create the next leaders then aligns them financially and strategically, which explains why neoclouds raise capital against hyperscaler competition and concedes that the position is granted rather than earned. The macro that dominated the last fortnight has eased rather than resolved. Anthropic's own economic scenario work, which he read this week, puts almost all of the divergence after 2027 — buildout years first, acceleration in 2028-2030 — which is a reasonable description of why the most rate-sensitive assets in this book move hardest in both directions.
keyPoints: Palantir names Nebius its preferred sovereign AI infrastructure partner
This is the company-specific catalyst the 1 Sep verdict said was missing
No disclosed contract value yet — a designation, not a revenue number
NVIDIA's sponsorship still explains the funding and concedes the position is granted
Anthropic's scenario work puts the divergence after 2027 — buildout first, acceleration 2028-2030

digests.narrative: The substrate layer had the week the desk was braced for, in both directions. Bloomberg reported that indium phosphide substrates are emerging as a key risk for the semiconductor industry — the exact chokepoint the analyst identified a year early through AXT. That is third-party validation of the thesis. It arrived alongside the risk that made the desk step AXT down to wait on 1 Sep: China reportedly halted some rare earth shipments to the United States, and Reuters' account named indium phosphide among the historical examples of what gets targeted, while Japan's imports of gallium, dysprosium, terbium and yttrium from China stood at zero in June. Shin-Etsu has suspended new orders for dysprosium magnets and Proterial had received no Chinese dysprosium export licences as of last month. Those are the mechanics of exactly the export-permit dependency AXT names in its own filings, being demonstrated on adjacent materials in real time. The read is that scarcity pricing and jurisdiction risk are the same story rather than competing ones: the material gets more valuable and harder to move at the same time, which is why the desk holds AXT at wait despite gross margin moving from 8.0% to 44.9%. The cleanest expression may be the non-Chinese supply — IQE sits in photonics in this book but is the epiwafer half of the same shortage, and Soitec's photonics-SOI benefits directly from the 80% silicon photonics penetration Goldman now models. Amkor's separate constraint is unchanged and under-discussed: OSATs warn traditional packaging capacity could face a deficit above 20% by 2027, with wire bonding the bottleneck, and Powertech is reported fully booked into 2030.
keyPoints: Bloomberg: indium phosphide substrates emerging as a key risk for the semiconductor industry
China reportedly halted some rare earth shipments to the US; Reuters named InP among historical targets
Japan's gallium, dysprosium, terbium and yttrium imports from China stood at zero in June
AXT's own filings name Chinese export permits for InP wafers as a live uncertainty
Scarcity and jurisdiction risk are the same story — the material gets dearer and harder to move at once
Powertech advanced packaging reported fully booked into 2030; OSAT deficit above 20% warned by 2027

digests.narrative: Broadcom did two things this week that pull in opposite directions for this theme. It guided AI revenue to roughly $115bn in FY27 and $230bn in FY28, both near 100% growth and far above a street modelling about $180bn, and said it is on target to exceed $30 of earnings per share in fiscal 2028 — which at the current price is under twelve times forward. It also said AI networking revenue is expected to grow just as fast as XPUs over the next few years, which is the part this theme owns. Set against the desk's 1 Sep framing, that matters: coverage was opened at wait on the argument that NVIDIA's MediaTek investment was building rival ASIC sponsors and eroding Broadcom's incumbency. The competitive point stands, but a company guiding to double revenue twice does not have a demand problem, and the desk should stop leaning on erosion as the main reason to wait. The second thing Broadcom did is more useful to the rest of the book than to itself: its CEO said demand for lasers, whether EML or CW, is far surpassing supply across the industry, and said it while tripling its own laser capacity. That is one of the largest laser suppliers in the world confirming the shortage, which is why it appears in the photonics digest as well. Marvell's optical engineering CTO separately named Europe and Japan as examples for laser sourcing for silicon photonics modules, notably not the United States, where Lumentum, Coherent and AAOI are redirecting capacity internally. Amazon's warrant structure over roughly $4bn of Qualcomm, tied to as much as $60bn of custom silicon milestone revenue, sits alongside its existing positions in Marvell, Astera and AAOI.
keyPoints: Broadcom guides AI revenue to about $115bn FY27 and $230bn FY28, against a street near $180bn
On target to exceed $30 EPS in fiscal 2028 — under twelve times forward at the current price
AI networking expected to grow as fast as XPUs over the next few years
Broadcom's CEO: laser demand far surpasses supply, said while tripling its own laser capacity
Marvell's optical CTO named Europe and Japan for laser sourcing, not the US
Amazon takes warrants over roughly $4bn of Qualcomm, tied to up to $60bn of custom silicon revenue

digests.narrative:
This card changes shape this week: LPKF moves into the glass layer from materials, so the theme finally contains the name through which glass-substrate progress actually reaches the book. It is still only two tickers.

The news is a delay, and it is the analyst reporting a setback in his own theme, which is the kind of disclosure worth weighting heavily. Samsung Electro-Mechanics has delayed its semiconductor glass substrate investment on a bottleneck in customer reliability evaluations of prototypes, revising the start of operations to 2028, with SKC also pushing back. For an equipment supplier this is worse than it is for a substrate maker: the tool order lands before the line runs, so a customer moving its start date right moves LPKF's revenue with it, and there is no partial credit. The share price is down about 12% on the month, which is the market reading the same thing.

Corning remains the other half of the card and has not moved: its glass-bridge case rests on 2028 fibre array unit TAM rather than anything shipping, and co-packaged optics delay reports weigh on that and the FAU case together. Conviction stays low. Glass is a 2028-2029 layer on current evidence, and the datapoint that would change this card is a disclosed tool order from a named substrate customer with a delivery year attached — not another timeline article.
keyPoints: LPK.DE re-categorised into glass from materials — the layer now holds the equipment exposure directly
Samsung Electro-Mechanics delays glass substrate start of operations to 2028; SKC also pushes back
Equipment leads the line, so a customer's slip moves LPKF's revenue event with it
LPK.DE is down about 12% on the month against a flat tape
GLW's glass-bridge case still rests on 2028 FAU TAM rather than current shipments
What would change the card: a disclosed LIDE order from a named customer with a delivery year

digests.narrative: He treats humanoids as the next major theme after space and AI, and is explicit that he wants downstream leaders rather than component suppliers. He is personally trying to own as much of Agility Robotics as possible, arguing that its application-specific approach — already deployed in Amazon and Mercado Libre warehouses — is further along in commercialization than the general-purpose programmes, and that its robots do not need to do backflips to do packaging and delivery work. He uses the Chinese listings as the valuation argument: Unitree's public listing at a far larger market capitalisation shows demand for pure-play humanoids is bigger than public markets expected, and XPeng carving out its robotics unit at a $6.3bn-plus valuation points the same way. On Tesla he is directly sceptical, writing that Optimus is wrapped inside a trillion-dollar company so it is not the pure-play exposure he is pointing at, and separately that he does not think Tesla can pull off general purpose yet. On upstream suppliers he is deliberately absent: mass production numbers are still too small, so he is not allocating much to actuator and component names, and tempers even the more focused ones on scale grounds.
keyPoints: Wants downstream humanoid leaders, not upstream component suppliers, until volumes scale
Agility framed as ahead on commercialization via Amazon and Mercado Libre warehouse deployments
Chinese listings — Unitree, XPeng's robotics carve-out — used as the valuation read-across
Explicitly sceptical on Tesla: Optimus is not pure-play exposure and general purpose is unproven
Component suppliers tempered: scale is vastly different until humanoid volumes are massive

digests.narrative: The demand side kept escalating and the leader stopped going up, which is the week in one line. NVIDIA's position is that 70% growth is what it can supply and that unconstrained growth would exceed 100%, with roughly $1.3T of hyperscaler capex projected for 2027 — and the analyst notes that figure excludes SpaceX, so the true total may surprise. Its moat argument has shifted from architecture to procurement: long-term agreements across lasers and memory plus ecosystem equity investments, now including $3.5bn into MediaTek and the $12.93bn acquisition of Hugging Face, which he reads as the GitHub playbook applied to 18m developers and 3m models. Inference is now larger than training, having been roughly even eighteen months ago, which matters because inference is the workload hyperscaler ASICs were supposed to take. On the numbers this is the strongest set the theme has produced: Broadcom guiding AI revenue from the mid $50bn range to $230bn across two years, Microsoft, Google and Amazon all describing compute imbalances into next year, and Powertech packaging booked into 2030. The desk's caution is where it was on 1 Sep and nothing this week addressed it. NVIDIA's receivables are $63.1bn against $96.2bn of quarterly revenue with five customers holding 70%, terms now run 90 days to a year, and total commitments reach $366bn once cloud agreements, equity stakes and uncommenced leases are counted. A vendor financing its own buyers is a different risk from a vendor that cannot make enough.
keyPoints: NVIDIA: 70% growth is supply-constrained; unconstrained would exceed 100%
Roughly $1.3T hyperscaler capex projected for 2027, and that figure excludes SpaceX
Inference is now larger than training, having been roughly even eighteen months ago
$3.5bn into MediaTek and $12.93bn for Hugging Face — procurement and ecosystem as the moat
Receivables $63.1bn on $96.2bn quarterly revenue, five customers holding 70%
Total commitments reach $366bn once cloud, equity and uncommenced leases are counted

digests.narrative: The buyers spent the week locking up silicon and inputs rather than announcing models, and Amazon was the most active. It took warrants over roughly $4bn of Qualcomm tied to as much as $60bn of milestone revenue from a custom silicon partnership, adding to existing equity and warrant positions across AlChip, Marvell, Astera and AAOI. The analyst's observation is fair and slightly uncomfortable: Amazon is accumulating semiconductor exposure at a rate that makes it look more like a sector fund than a customer. Read alongside the reported Samsung arrangement reserving around 70% of memory capacity through 2031 with NVIDIA, Microsoft and Google as counterparties, the pattern across this group is buyers converting cash into contracted supply and supplier equity — which is rational when the constraint is supply, and which also means their capex figures understate their commitment. Microsoft, Google and Amazon have all described compute imbalances running into next year. The timing question is the one worth holding. Anthropic's economic scenario publication, which he read closely, shows little separation through 2026-2027 and sharp divergence into 2028-2030, mapping onto the free-cash-flow headwinds these companies are absorbing now against projected profitability later. Alphabet's TPU v9 is named as another substantial source of optical demand, which is the same story arriving from the demand side.
keyPoints: Amazon takes warrants over roughly $4bn of Qualcomm, tied to up to $60bn of milestone revenue
Amazon now holds equity or warrants across AlChip, Marvell, Astera and AAOI
Samsung reportedly reserved about 70% of memory capacity to 2031 with NVIDIA, Microsoft and Google
Microsoft, Google and Amazon all describe compute imbalances running into next year
Google's TPU v9 named as another substantial source of optical demand
Anthropic's scenarios put little separation through 2027, sharp divergence into 2028-2030

digests.narrative:
This layer exists because the desk built it, not because the feed produced it. Every thesis that touches power reaches it through a list rather than an argument. Bloom Energy is the only sustained name: it appears in a late-July recap for 166% year-on-year revenue growth with expanding margins and raised 2026 guidance, and again in the note that grid power bottlenecks triggered a five-fold increase, to $25B, in Brookfield's financing for its fuel cells. That financing line is the clearest power-constraint datapoint anywhere in the feed.

The second thread is a components one and sits mostly outside the US listed set: a shortage of high-power cylindrical cells for battery backup units, with Samsung SDI supplying Simplo, which assembles for Meta and Amazon, and both Panasonic and Samsung reported short. Vertiv, Eaton, EnerSys and BorgWarner are named only as adjacent read-throughs, and the analyst says plainly it is outside his domain.

GE Vernova and Constellation carry no analyst mentions at all, which is exactly the tiering caveat this layer was built to expose: grid interconnection, transformers and on-site generation are load-bearing for every gigawatt in the neocloud and hyperscaler digests, and the feed prices none of it. Conviction is low because the evidence is thin, not because the constraint is.
keyPoints: Desk-built layer: no thesis in the feed argues power directly, only in passing
BE is the only sustained name — 166% YoY revenue growth, raised 2026 guidance
Grid power bottlenecks drove a 5x increase, to $25B, in Brookfield's financing for BE fuel cells
A BBU cylindrical-cell shortage runs through Samsung SDI, Panasonic and Murata, with no direct US listing
VRT, ETN and ENS appear only as adjacent read-throughs, explicitly outside the analyst's domain
GEV and CEG carry zero analyst mentions, so they cannot rise above radar however load-bearing they are
